name: Counting the Number of Valid and Banned Product Codes (Case 1)
description: Suppose a hypothetical company uses codes to represent its various products. A product code includes, among other information, a character in the tenth position that represents the zone from which that product was made. Due to some reorganization, products from zone R are banned from being sold.\nConstruct a program that reads product codes from the user and counts the number of valid and banned codes entered. Make sure that the program handles all possible exceptions.\nThe program must ask the user for an input until the user enters STOP.
code:
#Step 1: Define the function
def check_product_code():
    #Step 1.1: Assign initial values to the variables that we need for counts 
    valid = 0
    banned = 0
    #Step 1.2: Ask for a valid input as long as the user does'nt enter STOP; otherwise stop
    code = input("Enter product code: ")
    while ( code != "STOP") :
        #Step 1.2.1: Enclose the code that might throw an exception within the try block
        try : 
            zone = code[9]
            valid += 1
            if zone == "R" :
                banned += 1
        #Step 1.2.2: Handle all possible exceptions that may be thrown in the try block 
        except IndexError :                        
            print("Improper code length.")
        code = input("Enter product code: ")
    #Step 1.3: Print the result    
    print("# of valid codes entered:", valid)
    print("# of banned codes entered:", banned)
#Step 2: Call the function
check_product_code()

Best practices: You should strip whitespace and optionally normalize case so STOP and zone checks are robust, for example code = input(...).strip().upper() (then compare to 'STOP' or check the 10th char in a case-insensitive way). Also consider catching EOFError/KeyboardInterrupt around input() to handle unexpected user termination cleanly.

Alternative structure tip: Another clear pattern is to use a while True loop and immediately test the freshly read code for 'STOP' (and break) before attempting to access code[9]; this keeps the sentinel check next to the input and reduces subtle ordering bugs.

20.content: print("# of valid codes entered:", valid)
commentList: Purpose: This line prints the final number of codes that your program considered "valid" after the input loop finishes. It shows the user the result of the counting work you did in the loop.

Syntax and semantics: print(...) calls Python's print function. The first argument is a string literal "# of valid codes entered:" and the second argument is the variable valid. Because they are passed as separate arguments (separated by a comma), Python will convert valid to text if needed and insert a single space between the string and the number when it prints them, then end the line with a newline.

Common misconceptions and errors: if you tried to join the label and the number with the + operator like "..." + valid you would get a TypeError because you can't add a string and an int. Also be aware that if valid had not been defined earlier you would get a NameError — but in this program valid is defined at the top. Another possible confusion: this line only displays whatever value valid currently holds; if your counting logic is wrong (for example, the code increments valid before checking for a banned zone), the printed number will reflect that logic, not an independently verified count.

Best practices: you can make the output clearer and harder to break by using an f-string: print(f"# of valid codes entered: {valid}"). You might also handle singular/plural wording ("1 code" vs "2 codes") for nicer output, and keep this print after the loop so you only show results once all input is processed.

commentList: This line actually runs the program: by writing check_product_code() you invoke the function that prompts the user, reads codes in a loop, and prints the counts.

Syntactically this is a function call — the name followed by parentheses — and because there are no arguments in the definition you must call it with empty parentheses; omitting the parentheses would give you the function object instead of executing it.

If the function name were misspelled or not defined before this line, you would get a NameError at runtime, so you must ensure the def check_product_code(): line is present and correctly spelled above this call.

The function returns None (you don’t capture a return value here); any uncaught exceptions raised inside the function will propagate and may stop the program, even though IndexError is handled inside the function.
A common best practice is to protect this call with if __name__ == '__main__': check_product_code() so the code does not run automatically when the file is imported as a module.

Remember that each time you call the function the counters are reinitialized, so if you need cumulative counts across calls you would change the design; also consider separating input/output from logic to make testing easier.

distractors.description: You might select this because many languages use ++ to increase a variable by one and it looks shorter. However, in this language this is not a valid standalone statement for incrementing a variable. If you put this line in the program, the interpreter will raise a syntax error and the program will stop before it can continue asking for codes or print counts. In other words, this choice breaks execution rather than silently producing a wrong numeric result. The mistake here is treating the language as if it had a post/pre-increment operator; that assumption causes a runtime failure instead of the intended update of the counter.

You might pick this because you associate problems with user input with ValueError, or you remember ValueError from other exercises and think it will catch anything that goes wrong with the input. However, the specific error that happens when you try to access a character beyond the end of a string is a different runtime exception, so this handler will not run when that happens. As a result, if a user enters a too-short code the program will raise an uncaught error and stop instead of printing the "Improper code length." message and continuing to ask for input. Using this line therefore leaves the actual out-of-range indexing error unhandled and makes the program crash in the common failure case. The distractor is plausible because it is a real exception type, but it is the wrong one for the situation.

You might pick a bare except because it looks like the simplest way to catch any error. But this catches everything, including low-level and system-exiting exceptions, and will also swallow interrupts that the user might expect to work (like stopping the program). By catching every possible exception, you again hide the real cause of failures and respond to very different problems with the same message about code length. This can make the program behave unpredictably and makes it much harder for you to find and fix real bugs. Using a bare except is generally discouraged because it is too blunt and can prevent proper error handling and program termination.
